options: narrow line, high value added quadrant
broad line, high value added quadrant
broad line, low value added quadrant
narrow line, low value added quadrant
questions.explanation: One product line (jewellery) = narrow; prestige, location and service = high value added, the Tiffany quadrant. Broad line/high value added is for department stores carrying many lines.

questions.stem: ShoeSaver sells only discount footwear from plain stores in low-rent plazas, with self-service racks and no fitting help. On the retail positioning matrix, ShoeSaver sits in the:
options: broad line, high value added quadrant
broad line, low value added quadrant
narrow line, low value added quadrant
narrow line, high value added quadrant
questions.explanation: A single line (shoes) = narrow; plain stores, low-rent locations and no service = low value added, the Payless ShoeSource-style quadrant. Broad line/low value added (Walmart, Costco) requires many product lines.

questions.stem: A classmate says the retail positioning matrix compares retailers on price and quality. Which correction is accurate?
options: The axes are depth of line and markup percentage
The axes are breadth of product line and value added, where value added includes location, product reliability, prestige and service
The axes are level of service and form of ownership
The axes are target market size and number of stores
questions.explanation: Breadth of product line and value added are the matrix dimensions; price is an outcome, not an axis. Service is part of value added, but form of ownership is a separate way of classifying outlets, not a matrix dimension.

questions.stem: Northern Lux, a narrow-line luxury handbag retailer with high value added, wants to move into the broad line, high value added quadrant. What should it do?
options: Add many more product lines, such as clothing, shoes and cosmetics, while keeping its prestige and service
Cut service and prices while continuing to sell only handbags
Cut service and prices while adding many product lines
Narrow its line further to a single handbag brand
questions.explanation: Moving from narrow to broad means adding product lines; staying high value added means keeping prestige, location and service. Cutting service and prices while adding lines would land Northern Lux in the broad line, low value added quadrant instead.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT an element of 'value added' on the retail positioning matrix?
questions.explanation: Value added includes elements such as location, product reliability, prestige and service. Breadth of product line is the matrix's OTHER axis, not part of value added.

questions.stem: Graham's Spice LLC makes use of _____, which includes use of traditional media, new media, direct marketing, loyalty, and trade promotion to understand when and where its customers first think about purchasing its spices.
questions.explanation: Shopper marketing is a discipline for understanding how consumers behave as shoppers in different channels and formats; it reaches back to the time and place a consumer first thinks about buying and is by necessity multichannel. Retail positioning is how a retailer wants to be perceived, not a study of when and where shoppers start their purchase journey.

questions.stem: Shopper marketing is best defined as:
options: a discipline designed to understand how consumers behave as shoppers in different channels and formats
how a retailer wants to be perceived by consumers relative to competitors
assigning a manager responsibility for the profitability of a product category
selling brand-name merchandise below regular prices
questions.explanation: That is the course definition of shopper marketing. The distractors define retail positioning, category management and off-price retailing, three neighbouring retail concepts often confused with it.

questions.stem: Why is shopper marketing described as 'by necessity' a multichannel practice?
options: It can only be used by retailers that also operate catalogues
It focuses solely on in-store displays and signage
It requires manufacturers to sell through several types of wholesalers
It extends beyond the store to wherever and whenever consumers first think about purchasing, so it must reach them through many touchpoints
questions.explanation: Because shopper marketing follows the shopper from the first thought of buying (on social media, in a flyer, at the shelf), it relies on traditional media, new media, direct marketing, loyalty, trade promotion and in-store tools. Saying it focuses solely on in-store displays contradicts its defining feature of extending outside the store.

questions.stem: Brightwater Foods studies where customers are when they first think about buying granola (scrolling social media, reading a flyer, standing at the shelf) and coordinates digital ads, loyalty offers and in-store displays accordingly. A colleague calls this category management. Why is the colleague wrong?
options: It is retail positioning, because it concerns how the brand is perceived
It is shopper marketing; category management gives one manager profit responsibility for a product category
It is the wheel of retailing, because the firm is adding services
It is intertype competition, because several channels are involved
questions.explanation: Studying shopper behaviour across channels from the first moment of purchase consideration is shopper marketing. Category management is an internal structure in which a manager runs a category (e.g., snacks) as a strategic business unit; it does not describe tracking shoppers across media.

questions.stem: Which statement about shopper marketing is NOT accurate?
options: It extends to the time and place a consumer first thinks about purchasing
It uses traditional media, new media, direct marketing, loyalty and trade promotion
It examines how consumers behave in different channels and formats
It is limited to activities that take place inside the retail store
questions.explanation: Shopper marketing deliberately extends WELL OUTSIDE the store, to the point where a consumer first thinks about buying. The other three statements come straight from the course definition.

questions.stem: A retailer's year-end review shows $85,000 lost to shoplifting, damaged goods and paperwork errors. In the retailing mix figure, this issue falls in which quadrant?
questions.explanation: Shrinkage (theft, breakage, paperwork errors) is listed in the retail pricing mix alongside markups, markdowns and image/quality/value, because losses must be covered through pricing. It is not part of the products and services mix, even though the lost items are products.

questions.stem: Urban Pantry is deciding whether to open 12 small-format stores or 4 large ones and how to route deliveries from its warehouse to each store. These decisions fall in which part of the retailing mix?
questions.explanation: Number of stores, store size, format and logistics are all elements of the physical location mix. The products and services mix covers assortment, service and guarantees, not how many stores to run or how goods reach them.

questions.stem: BrightNest Home introduces a 90-day no-questions exchange policy and debates dropping free in-home design consultations to keep costs down. These decisions belong to which retailing mix quadrant?
questions.explanation: Guarantees and exchanges and product-service trade-offs are listed under the products and services mix. The pricing mix is tempting because cost is mentioned, but the decisions themselves are about which services to offer, not markups or markdowns.

questions.stem: According to the chapter, what is the main purpose of a retailer's communications mix?
options: To set markups, markdowns and allowances for shrinkage
To choose between strip locations and power centres
To communicate the retailer's unique benefits using integrated, multiple channels
To determine the breadth and depth of the merchandise mix
questions.explanation: The communications mix exists to communicate unique benefits, ideally through integrated, multiple channels (the Indigo example: stores, website, email, loyalty and social media working together). The other options belong to the pricing, location and products and services quadrants.

questions.stem: Which element does NOT belong in the communications mix quadrant of the retailing mix?
questions.explanation: Markdowns belong in the retail pricing mix. The communications quadrant includes personal selling, advertising, displays and signage, public relations, catalogues, telephone sales and follow-up, website, direct marketing and database marketing.

questions.stem: Which element is correctly matched with its retailing mix quadrant?
options: Sales functions and assistance: retail pricing mix
Image, quality and value: retail pricing mix
questions.explanation: The pricing quadrant lists image, quality and value along with markups, markdowns and shrinkage, because price signals image. Catalogues are in the communications mix, logistics in the physical location mix, and sales functions and assistance in the products and services mix.

questions.stem: In the course's retailing mix figure, what is at the centre of the four quadrants, and what surrounds the whole mix?
options: The target market and consumers are at the centre, surrounded by information
Price is at the centre, surrounded by the other three quadrants
The wholesaler is at the centre, surrounded by suppliers
Store atmosphere is at the centre, surrounded by communications
questions.explanation: All four quadrants (products and services, pricing, physical location, communications) are arranged around the target market and consumers, and information surrounds the mix. Price is only one quadrant, not the hub.

questions.stem: A retailer's merchandise mix is best described as:
options: how many different products a store carries, and in what assortment
how many different types of products a store carries, and how they are displayed
what assortment of products a store expects to stock annually
the products a store is considering purchasing for the coming quarter of the business cycle
questions.explanation: The merchandise mix describes how many different types of products a store carries and in what assortment. How products are displayed relates to store atmosphere, not the merchandise mix, which is why the second option is wrong.

questions.stem: TrendHouse carries four product lines: shoes (60 items), appliances (25 items), CDs (300 titles) and men's clothing (90 items). What is the BREADTH of TrendHouse's merchandise mix?
questions.explanation: Breadth = the number of different product lines carried = 4 (shoes, appliances, CDs, men's clothing). 475 is the total item count (60 + 25 + 300 + 90 = 475), and 300 is the depth of the CD line, not breadth.

questions.stem: Store X carries 3 product lines with about 500 items in each. Store Y carries 40 product lines with about 10 items in each. Which statement is correct?
options: Store X has the deeper merchandise mix; Store Y has the broader one
Store X has the broader merchandise mix; Store Y has the deeper one
Both stores have the same breadth because their totals are similar
Store Y is deeper because it carries more product lines
questions.explanation: Breadth counts the number of product lines (Y = 40 vs X = 3), while depth counts items within each line (X = 500 vs Y = 10). So X is deeper and Y is broader; mixing these up is the most common trap.

questions.stem: Tackle Box Outdoors adds 40 new fishing lures to its existing fishing line without adding any new product lines. Which aspect of its merchandise mix has changed?
questions.explanation: Adding items within an existing line increases depth, the number of items in each product line. Breadth would change only if Tackle Box added a new line (e.g., camping gear).

questions.stem: A retailer's merchandise mix does NOT describe which of the following?
options: How products are displayed and lit in the store
The number of different product lines carried
The number of items within each product line
The assortment offered within its lines
questions.explanation: Display and lighting are store atmosphere decisions. The merchandise mix covers how many types of products (breadth) and in what assortment (depth) a store carries.

questions.stem: Category management involves:
options: a big-box retailer dominating one category with deep assortment and low prices
assigning a manager responsibility for the profitability of a product category and managing it as a strategic business unit
classifying retail outlets by the breadth of lines they carry
understanding how consumers behave as shoppers across channels
questions.explanation: Category management makes one manager accountable for a category's profitability (e.g., shoes) and runs it like a strategic business unit. The first distractor describes a category killer, a store format, and the last describes shopper marketing.

questions.stem: At FreshCo Markets, one manager is responsible for the entire snack category: choosing brands, allocating shelf space, planning promotions and answering for the category's profit. This approach is called:
questions.explanation: Giving one manager profit responsibility for a whole product category and running it as a strategic business unit is category management. 'Category killer' sounds similar but is a type of discount specialty store, not an internal management approach.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes category management from a category killer?
options: A category killer is how a retailer manages product categories internally; category management is a store format
Both are store formats classified by depth of line
Category management is an internal way to manage product categories; a category killer is a store format with deep, low-priced assortment in one category
Both are forms of retail ownership
questions.explanation: Category management is a management practice (one manager, one category, profit responsibility); a category killer (Best Buy, Staples) is a type of store. The reversed option swaps them.

questions.stem: What is a key benefit of category management for a retailer?
options: Treating each category as a strategic business unit aligns its assortment with the target market and clarifies profit responsibility
It eliminates shrinkage from the category
It removes the need to select a target market
It turns the retailer into a merchant wholesaler
questions.explanation: By making a manager accountable for a category's profitability, category management helps align the assortment with what the target market wants. It does not eliminate shrinkage or replace target market selection, which still comes first.

questions.stem: A Calgary grocer notices its baby-products aisle is cluttered with slow-selling brands, and no one can say whether the aisle makes money. Applying category management, the grocer should:
options: open a separate big-box baby store with very low prices
add unrelated products such as hardware to the aisle
appoint one manager to run baby products as a strategic business unit, adjusting the assortment to target customers and profit
replace the aisle with self-service vending machines
questions.explanation: Category management means one manager owns the category's profitability and tunes its assortment to the target market. Opening a big-box discount baby store would be launching a category killer, a different concept entirely.

questions.stem: Cedar & Sage, a home decor store, plays soft acoustic music, uses warm lighting and diffuses a faint cedar scent to create a calm, upscale impression. Which element of the retailing mix is Cedar & Sage managing?
questions.explanation: Music, lighting, scent and layout are atmospherics that shape the overall impression of the store. The merchandise mix is about which product lines and assortments are carried, which this scenario does not change.

questions.stem: Store atmosphere refers to:
options: the overall impression a store conveys through elements such as layout, lighting, music and scent
the number of product lines a store carries and its assortment
the services a store offers before and after a purchase
a store's position on the breadth-of-line and value-added matrix
questions.explanation: Store atmosphere (atmospherics) is the overall impression created by sensory and design elements. The distractors describe the merchandise mix, prepurchase and postpurchase services, and the retail positioning matrix.

questions.stem: A clothing retailer changes its layout, colour scheme and lighting but keeps exactly the same products and staffing. Which element of its products and services mix has changed?
questions.explanation: Layout, colour and lighting are atmospheric elements, so store atmosphere has changed. The merchandise mix (types and assortment of products) and level of service (staffing and services) were explicitly left unchanged.

questions.stem: Why do retailers invest in store atmosphere?
options: It creates the overall impression that shapes the store's image and supports its positioning
It reduces the number of product lines the store must carry
It replaces the need for a communications mix
It allows the store to take title to goods it never handles
questions.explanation: Atmosphere provides the overall impression customers form of the store, reinforcing its retail image and positioning (calm and upscale vs fast and bargain-focused). It does not change the merchandise mix or substitute for communications.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT an atmospheric element of a store?
questions.explanation: Markup is a retail pricing decision. Atmospherics are sensory and design elements such as layout, music, lighting and scent that create the overall impression of a store.

questions.stem: Ridgeview Sports cuts the price of last season's unsold snowboards by 40% to clear them out before spring. This price reduction is a:
questions.explanation: A markdown is a reduction in the selling price to move slow or seasonal merchandise. Off-price retailing is a whole strategy of selling brand names below regular prices using manufacturers' excess inventory, not a one-time cut on a store's own stock.

questions.stem: A convenience store's year-end count shows $3,200 less merchandise than its records, due to shoplifting, broken items and recording errors. This loss is called:
questions.explanation: Shrinkage is inventory lost to theft, breakage and paperwork errors, and it is part of the retail pricing mix. Risk bearing is a WHOLESALER function (absorbing ownership risk), not the retail term for these losses.

questions.stem: A retailer buys a jacket for $60 and sells it for $75. What is the markup as a percentage of the selling price?
questions.explanation: Markup on selling price = (price - cost) / price = ($75 - $60) / $75 = $15 / $75 = 20%. 25% is the markup on COST ($15 / $60), and 80% is cost as a share of price ($60 / $75).

questions.stem: Harbour Home marks down a coffee maker from $120 to $90. By what percentage of the original price was it reduced?
questions.explanation: Markdown = $120 - $90 = $30; $30 / $120 (original price) = 25%. 33% is the trap of dividing by the new price ($30 / $90), and 75% is the new price as a share of the original ($90 / $120).

questions.stem: How does a markdown differ from off-price retailing?
options: A markdown sells brand names from manufacturers' excess inventory; off-price retailing reduces prices on slow stock
Both are forms of shrinkage caused by theft and breakage
A markdown reduces the price of a retailer's own slow-moving stock; off-price retailing sells brand names below regular prices by buying manufacturers' excess inventory
A markdown raises the selling price; off-price retailing lowers it
questions.explanation: Markdowns are price cuts to move slow merchandise; off-price retailing (Winners, Costco, outlets) is an ongoing business model based on buying excess inventory. The reversed option swaps the two, and neither is shrinkage.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT listed in the retail pricing mix?
questions.explanation: The retail pricing mix lists image, quality and value; markups; markdowns; and shrinkage. Store layout belongs elsewhere: it is part of store atmosphere and of the size-and-layout decisions in the physical location mix.

questions.stem: Off-price retailing is best described as:
options: selling brand-name merchandise at lower than regular prices, often by buying manufacturers' excess inventory
temporarily reducing the price of a store's own slow-moving stock
adding several unrelated product lines to a single store
selling only private-label goods at full price
questions.explanation: Off-price retailers (warehouse clubs, outlet stores, single-price/extreme-value stores, off-price chains) build their model on brand names below regular prices. A temporary price cut on slow stock is a markdown, not off-price retailing.

questions.stem: Bargain Boulevard buys designer-brand clothing and home goods that manufacturers overproduced or other retailers cancelled, and sells them at 20-60% below department-store prices. Bargain Boulevard is a(n):
questions.explanation: Off-price chains such as Winners buy brand-name excess inventory and sell it below regular prices. A warehouse club also sells for less, but it charges a membership fee and focuses on food and general merchandise in bulk.

questions.stem: BulkWay charges an annual membership fee and sells food and general merchandise in large package sizes from no-frills warehouse stores. BulkWay is a(n):
questions.explanation: Membership fees, bulk packages and no-frills warehouse stores mark a warehouse club (Costco). A hypermarket also combines groceries and general merchandise, but it has no membership model and is not an off-price format.

questions.stem: Northern Parka operates its own stores in a factory outlet mall, selling its excess inventory and discontinued styles at reduced prices. These stores are:
questions.explanation: Outlet stores let a manufacturer sell its OWN excess and discontinued stock at reduced prices. Off-price chains buy other manufacturers' excess inventory; a sales office is a manufacturer's wholesaling unit that sells to businesses, not consumers.

questions.stem: Loonie Land sells party supplies, kitchen gadgets and snacks at one or a few fixed low price points, with nothing over $5. Loonie Land is a(n):
questions.explanation: Single-price/extreme-value stores (Dollarama is the course example) sell at one or a few fixed low price points. An off-price chain sells brand-name apparel and home goods below regular prices but not at fixed price points.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a type of off-price retailer?
questions.explanation: The four off-price types are warehouse clubs, outlet stores, single-price/extreme-value stores and off-price chains. A full-service department store sells at regular prices with many services.

questions.stem: What BEST distinguishes a warehouse club from an off-price chain?
options: A warehouse club is full-service; an off-price chain is self-service
An off-price chain is a contractual system; a warehouse club is a corporate chain
A warehouse club charges membership and sells food and general merchandise in bulk; an off-price chain sells brand-name goods bought from excess inventory
A warehouse club is a category killer; an off-price chain is a hypermarket
questions.explanation: Both are off-price formats, but Costco-style clubs rely on memberships and bulk food and general merchandise, while Winners-style chains sell brand-name fashion and home goods from manufacturers' excess inventory. The other options mix in unrelated classification schemes (service level, ownership, merchandise line).

questions.stem: Stephen Avenue Books is located in downtown Calgary among office towers, banks and transit stops, where thousands of workers walk past daily. This location type is a:
questions.explanation: The central business district is the downtown area of a city, with heavy foot traffic from office workers. A strip location is a cluster of stores along a busy street serving a neighbourhood.

questions.stem: Kingsgate Centre is a large mall of about 120 stores anchored by two department stores, drawing shoppers from across the city and surrounding towns. Kingsgate is a:
questions.explanation: Regional shopping centres have roughly 50-150 stores with department-store anchors and draw from a wide area. A community centre is smaller: one primary store plus 20-40 smaller stores.

questions.stem: Maplewood Plaza has one primary store, a large supermarket, plus about 30 smaller shops serving several nearby neighbourhoods. Maplewood Plaza is a:
questions.explanation: One primary store plus 20-40 smaller stores defines a community shopping centre. A regional centre is larger (50-150 stores) and anchored by department stores.

questions.stem: A dry cleaner, a pizza place, a nail salon, a convenience store and a pharmacy sit side by side along a busy neighbourhood street, each with parking out front. This is a:
questions.explanation: A strip location is a cluster of stores along a busy street serving everyday neighbourhood needs. It is not a community shopping centre because there is no primary anchor store with 20-40 smaller stores.

questions.stem: South Ridge Commons is a huge open-air strip of big-box stores anchored by several national retailers, including an electronics category killer, a home-improvement warehouse and a discount supercentre. South Ridge is a:
questions.explanation: A power centre is a huge shopping strip with several national anchor stores, often category killers. A plain strip location has small neighbourhood stores rather than multiple national big-box anchors.

questions.stem: The Promenade is an open-air centre with upscale boutiques, restaurants, landscaped walkways and a cinema, designed to feel like a pedestrian village. The Promenade is a:
questions.explanation: Lifestyle centres are open-air, upscale centres mixing specialty shops with dining and entertainment. A power centre is also open-air, but it is built around big-box national anchors and category killers, not upscale boutiques and leisure.

questions.stem: What distinguishes a power centre from a regional shopping centre?
options: A power centre has one primary store and 20-40 smaller stores; a regional centre is a downtown business district
A power centre is a huge strip anchored by national big-box stores or category killers; a regional centre has 50-150 stores with department-store anchors
A power centre is an upscale open-air village; a regional centre is a small neighbourhood strip
Both are names for downtown shopping areas
questions.explanation: Anchors are the key: power centres cluster big-box national anchors and category killers in a giant strip, while regional centres have 50-150 stores anchored by department stores. One primary store plus 20-40 smaller ones describes a community centre.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a physical location decision in the retailing mix?
options: Choosing the type of shopping area to locate in
Deciding how many stores to operate
Deciding whether to sell through non-store channels such as mail
questions.explanation: Markdowns belong to the retail pricing mix. Physical location covers where to locate, the number of stores, store size, format and logistics, and non-store options such as mail.

questions.stem: Lumen Home, an upscale decor boutique, targets affluent shoppers who like to browse, dine and linger. It wants to sit among similar upscale shops and restaurants in an attractive open-air setting. Which location type fits Lumen Home BEST?
questions.explanation: A lifestyle centre is an open-air, upscale centre mixing specialty shops with dining and entertainment, a match for Lumen's target market. A power centre is also open-air, but it is built around big-box national anchors and category killers that attract bargain-focused trips, not lingering affluent browsers.

questions.stem: Which statement is TRUE of non-store retailing?
options: Non-store retailing describes small, mobile retail activities like door-to-door sales and food carts
Non-store retailing occurs outside and may be impacted by weather or other environmental forces
Non-store retailing comprises activities of varying levels of customer and retailer involvement, outside the store environment
Non-store retailing refers specifically to buying goods and services via automated or electronic means
questions.explanation: Non-store retailing occurs outside a retail outlet through activities involving varying levels of customer and retailer involvement: automatic vending, direct mail and catalogues, TV home shopping, online retailing, telemarketing and direct selling. The 'automated or electronic' option is too narrow, because direct selling and telemarketing are non-store but involve people, and the first option wrongly limits it to small mobile activities.

questions.stem: Glow Beauty sells skin-care products through independent consultants who host parties in customers' homes and demonstrate the products. This form of non-store retailing is:
questions.explanation: Direct selling involves personal contact with consumers in their homes or offices, door-to-door or through in-home parties (Avon, Tupperware). Telemarketing also involves personal contact, but by phone, not face to face.

questions.stem: Huckleberry Books, which has run stores across Canada for decades, launches a website and app so shoppers can order books for home delivery. Huckleberry has become a:
questions.explanation: A traditional bricks-and-mortar retailer that also engages in non-store retailing (here online) becomes a click-and-mortar retailer. A category killer is about deep, low-price assortment in one category, which the scenario does not mention.

questions.stem: SnackSmart places machines in Edmonton hospitals and campus buildings that sell healthy snacks and drinks 24 hours a day with no staff present. This form of retailing is:
questions.explanation: Automatic vending is non-store retailing through machines that sell without salespeople. Direct selling requires personal, face-to-face contact with consumers.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a form of non-store retailing?
options: Operating a store in a strip location
questions.explanation: A strip location is a type of physical store location, so it is store-based retailing. Non-store forms are automatic vending, direct mail and catalogues, TV home shopping, online retailing, telemarketing and direct selling.

questions.stem: Which pairing of non-store retailing form and example is correct?
options: Television home shopping: a channel showcasing products that viewers order by phone or online
Telemarketing: a consultant demonstrating cookware at a home party
Direct selling: a call centre phoning households to sell insurance
Direct mail and catalogues: a machine dispensing phone chargers in an airport
questions.explanation: TV home shopping displays products on television for viewers to order. The other pairings are swapped: a home party is direct selling, a call centre is telemarketing, and a machine is automatic vending.

questions.stem: Fred uses the internet to research, compare, and decide on a new camera at his own pace. This demonstrates the online shopping benefit of:
questions.explanation: Online shoppers are empowered consumers: they seek information, evaluate alternatives and decide on their own time, terms and conditions, which is the CONTROL benefit of the six Cs. 'Limited control' and 'reliance on in-store salespeople' describe the opposite of what Fred is doing.

questions.stem: Dell Computers allows online shoppers to choose the components in their computer instead of buying one off the shelf. This exemplifies:
questions.explanation: Choosing your own components tailors the product to you, which is the customization benefit. Control is the tempting distractor, but control is about deciding at your own pace and on your own terms, not configuring the product itself.

questions.stem: Priya, a nurse working night shifts, orders groceries online at 3 a.m. from home because no store is open when she is free. Which of the six Cs does this illustrate?
questions.explanation: Convenience means shopping 24/7 from anywhere, without store hours or travel. Control is about researching and deciding at your own pace and on your own terms; Priya's motive is timing and access, not decision power.

questions.stem: Marcus could not find size-15 hiking boots in any Calgary store, but online he found 40 styles from dozens of brands, plus a size-finder tool to help him narrow them down. Which of the six Cs does this illustrate?
questions.explanation: Choice is the broad selection (plus assistance) available online, far beyond any local store's shelves. Customization would mean the boots were configured or personalized for Marcus, not simply picked from a larger range.

questions.stem: Before buying a stroller online, Lena chats live with a company representative, emails a question about safety ratings and reads the brand's replies to her comments on Instagram. Which of the six Cs does this illustrate?
questions.explanation: Communication covers two-way interaction online: email, live chat, reviews and social media. Control is tempting, but Lena's experience centres on exchanging messages with the company, not on deciding alone at her own pace.

questions.stem: Ahmed uses a price-comparison site to find the lowest price on a gaming headset and saves $40 compared with the mall. Which of the six Cs does this illustrate?
questions.explanation: Cost refers to lower prices and the ease of comparing them online. Choice is about the breadth of selection, while Ahmed's goal is clearly to save money.

questions.stem: Which scenario BEST illustrates the CONTROL benefit of online shopping rather than CONVENIENCE?
options: Jen orders a birthday gift at midnight because the website never closes
Tasha shops online from her cottage, hours from the nearest mall
Ben buys a desk lamp on his phone while riding the bus
Omar researches laptop specs on several sites over two weeks and decides on his own terms, without a salesperson
questions.explanation: Control = empowered consumers who search, evaluate and decide at their own pace and on their own terms. The other three are about WHEN and WHERE someone can shop, which is convenience.

questions.stem: Which scenario illustrates CUSTOMIZATION rather than CHOICE?
options: A shopper browses 3,000 sneaker styles from 50 brands
A shopper filters a huge catalogue by size to find in-stock styles
A shopper uses an online fit assistant to pick from hundreds of models
A shopper designs her own sneakers by picking the colours and materials and adding her initials
questions.explanation: Customization tailors the product itself to the individual (like Dell letting buyers choose components). Browsing or filtering a large existing selection, even with help, is the choice benefit.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the six Cs that explain why consumers shop online?
questions.explanation: The six Cs are convenience, choice, communication, customization, cost and control. 'Community' sounds plausible, but it is not on the course list.

questions.stem: According to the chapter, how do online reviews affect consumers?
options: They make consumers rely more heavily on in-store salespeople
They create smarter, more informed and more demanding consumers
They reduce the influence of other people's opinions
They make consumers less sensitive to price differences
questions.explanation: The slides state that reviews create smarter, more informed and demanding consumers, and that influencers' opinions are important. Reviews increase, not reduce, the role of other people's opinions.

questions.stem: According to the slides, online retailing allows consumers to do which three things?
questions.explanation: Online retailing supports search, evaluation (comparison) and purchase. 'Warehouse, transport and finance' are wholesaler functions, not consumer activities.

questions.stem: FitWear, an online activewear retailer, finds that visitors leave because they are unsure whether products will suit them and have no one to ask. Which change MOST directly strengthens the COMMUNICATION benefit of shopping online?
options: Adding live chat with fit specialists and showing customer reviews on every product page
Letting shoppers design their own custom leggings
Adding hundreds of new styles from other brands
questions.explanation: Communication covers two-way interaction (chat, email, reviews, social media), which directly answers 'no one to ask.' The other options strengthen cost, customization and choice, which do not address the communication gap.

questions.stem: Jimmy's, a multichannel retailer, assists customers to order items that may be out of stock at one of its retail stores. The customers may use the catalogue to place the order. This provision BEST illustrates that Jimmy's:
options: mainly has its retail outlets in the central business district
recognizes that the Internet is an effective relationship-building medium among different channel operations
benefits from the synergy of sharing information among its different channel operations
typically reduces the size of its target markets
questions.explanation: Multichannel retailers integrate store and non-store formats (catalogue, online); because the channels share information, a store can fill an out-of-stock order through the catalogue, which is the synergy of sharing information. The Internet option is tempting, but the scenario involves a catalogue and is about channels working together, not the Internet as a relationship medium.

questions.stem: Kai tries on ski boots at a Banff ski shop and gets fitted by the staff, then orders the same boots online from a cheaper seller. This behaviour is called:
questions.explanation: Showrooming = examining products in a store, then buying online. Webrooming is the reverse: researching online and then buying in a physical store.

questions.stem: Danielle reads reviews and compares blender prices online, then drives to a nearby store and buys the model she chose that afternoon. This behaviour is called:
questions.explanation: Webrooming = researching online, then buying in store; Danielle is a cross-channel shopper. Showrooming runs in the opposite direction (look in store, buy online).

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes showrooming from webrooming?
options: Showrooming means researching online and buying in a store; webrooming means examining in a store and buying online
Showrooming is done by retailers; webrooming is done by manufacturers
Showrooming means examining a product in a store and buying it online; webrooming means researching online and buying in a store
Both describe consumers who use only a single channel
questions.explanation: Both are cross-channel shopping behaviours: showrooming uses the store as a showroom for an online purchase; webrooming uses the web to research an in-store purchase. They are consumer behaviours, and by definition involve more than one channel.

questions.stem: Retailers that use and integrate a combination of traditional store and non-store formats, such as stores, catalogues and online retailing, are called:
questions.explanation: Multichannel retailers integrate store and non-store formats to offer a broader spectrum of benefits and experiences. A drop shipper is a limited-service wholesaler, and a category killer is a deep, low-price store format.

questions.stem: Why do many retailers adopt a multichannel strategy?
options: Multiple channels allow them to reduce the size of their target markets
Integrating channels lets them offer a broader spectrum of benefits and experiences and share information across channel operations
Multiple channels eliminate the need for any physical stores
Multiple channels stop consumers from shopping across channels
questions.explanation: Using several integrated channels lets retailers reach shoppers in more ways and gain synergy from shared information (as in the Jimmy's example). Shrinking the target market is the distractor from the official question; multichannel retailing typically widens reach.

questions.stem: Despite fast home delivery, Olivia drives to a store for a new phone charger because she wants to walk out with it right now rather than wait two days. Which reason that face-to-face (F2F) retail is 'not dead yet' does this illustrate?
questions.explanation: The slides list instant gratification, convenience, experience and savings as reasons F2F retail survives; wanting the item immediately is instant gratification. Nothing in the scenario involves saving money or an in-store experience.

questions.stem: According to the 2025 Retail Council of Canada / Adyen survey discussed in class, roughly what share of online shoppers reach checkout and then leave to compare shipping costs and prices on other sites?
questions.explanation: Nearly two-thirds of online shoppers make it to checkout and then leave to compare shipping costs and prices, a serious cart-abandonment threat. The 9% figure is the share who use a digital wallet.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a finding or recommendation from the retail trends survey (Retail Council of Canada / Adyen) discussed in class?
options: Most Canadian shoppers now pay with digital wallets rather than cards
Nearly two-thirds of online shoppers leave at checkout to compare shipping costs and prices
Only 9% use a digital wallet; most use debit or credit cards
Experiential tools such as Instagram storefronts, QR codes and GPS can improve online retailing
questions.explanation: Only 9% use a digital wallet and most pay by debit or credit card, so the claim that most use digital wallets is false. The other three statements match the survey slide.

questions.stem: Pine & Ply, an online furniture retailer, sees many shoppers reach checkout and then leave after seeing shipping costs. Based on the retail trends discussed in class, what threat is this, and what is a sensible response?
options: Showrooming; open more physical stores in power centres
Shrinkage; add security tags to inventory
Cart abandonment as shoppers leave to compare shipping and prices elsewhere; show competitive, transparent shipping costs early
Intertype competition; add unrelated product lines
questions.explanation: The survey found nearly two-thirds of online shoppers reach checkout, then leave to compare shipping costs and prices, so competitive, transparent shipping directly addresses the threat. Shrinkage is loss from theft, breakage and errors, which has nothing to do with abandoned carts.

questions.stem: Marco leaves a store without buying because the checkout line was 20 minutes long and the jacket he wanted was out of stock. Which point about the modern retail environment does this illustrate?
options: Consumers dislike long lines, poor customer service and stock-outs
The growth of social media purchasing
questions.explanation: The slides note that consumers dislike long lines, poor customer service and stock-outs, exactly what drove Marco away. The decline of middle-market retailers describes a market-wide squeeze on mid-priced chains, not one shopper's bad visit.

questions.stem: Mid-priced chains that are neither the cheapest option nor a premium experience are closing stores, while discounters and luxury retailers grow. Which modern retail trend does this describe?
questions.explanation: The slides list the decline of middle-market retailers as a feature of today's environment, as shoppers gravitate to either low prices or high-value experiences. The wheel of retailing describes how a single low-price entrant trades up over time, not a squeeze on the middle of the market.

questions.stem: Why does the chapter recommend experiential or interactive online features such as Instagram storefronts, QR codes and GPS tools?
options: To improve the online retailing experience and engage shoppers
To reduce the retailer's breadth of product line
To eliminate the need for debit and credit cards
To avoid holding inventory, as drop shippers do
questions.explanation: The survey slide suggests improving online retailing through experiential or interactive activities such as online social shopping (Instagram storefronts), QR codes and GPS. These tools engage shoppers; they do not change the product line or replace card payments (most shoppers still use debit or credit).

questions.stem: A small Edmonton boutique uses Shopify to sync inventory across its store, website and Instagram shop, so a customer can buy a sweater from an Instagram post and pick it up in store. Which modern retail theme does this BEST illustrate?
options: Technology-driven retail optimization supporting omnichannel and social media purchasing
questions.explanation: The slides highlight omnichannel and social media purchasing, the role of technology and retail optimization (Shopify is the course example). Nothing here involves selling brand names below regular prices (off-price) or adding unrelated lines (scrambled merchandising).

questions.stem: The wheel of retailing describes how:
options: retail outlets pass through early growth, accelerated development, maturity and decline
very dissimilar types of retail outlets compete for the same customers
new retail forms enter as low-status, low-margin, low-price outlets, gradually add services and raise prices, and leave room for new low-price entrants
retailers move from narrow product lines to broad ones
questions.explanation: That is the wheel of retailing. The first distractor describes the retail life cycle, the most commonly confused concept, and the second describes intertype competition.

questions.stem: QuickBurger began as a cheap walk-up burger stand. Over 30 years it added seating, drive-thrus, salads, premium coffee and renovated dining rooms, and its prices rose. Now no-frills food trucks undercut it on price. This pattern illustrates:
questions.explanation: Entering at low prices, trading up with services and higher prices, then being undercut by new low-price entrants is the wheel of retailing (the course's McDonald's example). The retail life cycle tracks the growth and decline of a format, not this trade-up-and-replace pattern.

questions.stem: Which observation fits the wheel of retailing rather than the retail life cycle?
options: A retail format's market share rises quickly, levels off and then falls
A format moves from early growth into accelerated development
Video-rental stores grow, mature and eventually close as streaming arrives
A discount chain upgrades its stores and services and raises prices, opening a gap for new low-price competitors
questions.explanation: The wheel is about trading UP in price, status and service, which creates room for new low-price entrants. Growth, levelling off and decline over time are stages of the retail life cycle.

questions.stem: In the wheel of retailing, what happens immediately after a new retailer enters the market as a low-status, low-margin, low-price outlet?
options: It gradually adds services and upgrades its facilities, raising prices and status
New low-price retailers enter beneath it
It cuts services further to become a hard discounter
questions.explanation: The sequence is: enter at low prices, then trade up (add services, raise prices and status), which leaves a gap that new low-price entrants fill. New entrants come only AFTER the incumbent has traded up.

questions.stem: According to the wheel of retailing, why do opportunities keep opening up for new discount retailers?
options: Established retailers trade up by adding services and raising prices, leaving a low-price gap
Consumers eventually refuse to shop at full-service stores
Category killers are forced out by regulation
Markups shrink to zero as retailers mature
questions.explanation: As incumbents add services and raise prices and status, they abandon the low-price position, and new low-margin entrants step into that gap. The other options are not part of the wheel concept.

questions.stem: The retail life cycle refers to:
options: new retail forms entering as low-price outlets and gradually trading up
the process of growth and decline that retail outlets, like products, experience
the steps a shopper follows from search to purchase
the sequence of functions a wholesaler performs
questions.explanation: The retail life cycle applies life-cycle thinking to retail outlets: they grow and then decline. Entering at low prices and trading up describes the wheel of retailing.

questions.stem: What is the correct sequence of the retail life cycle stages?
options: Early growth, accelerated development, maturity, decline
Accelerated development, early growth, maturity, decline
Early growth, maturity, accelerated development, decline
questions.explanation: The retail life cycle runs early growth, accelerated development, maturity, then decline. 'Introduction, growth, maturity, decline' is the PRODUCT life cycle, a common trap.

questions.stem: Video-rental chains spread rapidly in the 1980s and 1990s, peaked, then saw market share and profits collapse as streaming arrived, and most stores closed. This pattern best illustrates:
questions.explanation: A retail format growing, maturing and declining over time is the retail life cycle. Nothing here involves trading up in price and service, which is the wheel of retailing.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly contrasts the retail life cycle with the wheel of retailing?
options: The retail life cycle explains how low-price entrants trade up; the wheel of retailing tracks a format's growth and decline
The retail life cycle tracks a format's growth and decline over time; the wheel of retailing explains how low-price entrants trade up and get replaced
Both describe how individual consumers move from search to purchase
Both apply only to wholesalers, not retailers
questions.explanation: Life cycle = stages of growth and decline (early growth, accelerated development, maturity, decline). Wheel = the price and status trade-up dynamic that leaves room for new discounters. The reversed option swaps them.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a stage of the retail life cycle?
questions.explanation: The retail life cycle stages are early growth, accelerated development, maturity and decline. 'Introduction' is the first stage of the product life cycle, not the retail life cycle.

questions.stem: _____ includes all the activities in selling goods or services to those who buy for resale or business use.
questions.explanation: Wholesaling is defined by the buyer's purpose: resale or business use. Retailing sells to ultimate consumers for personal, family or household use.

questions.stem: Canuck Office Supply sells pallets of copy paper, toner and office furniture to schools, hospitals and law firms for use in their operations. Canuck Office Supply is engaged in:
questions.explanation: Selling to organizations that buy for business use is wholesaling, even though the schools and hospitals are the final users. Retailing requires ultimate consumers buying for personal, family or household use.

questions.stem: Which purchase is wholesaling rather than retailing?
options: A parent buying latex gloves for household cleaning
A dentist buying boxes of latex gloves for her clinic
A student buying winter gloves for a ski trip
A retiree renting a snowblower to clear his driveway
questions.explanation: The dentist buys for business use, which makes the sale wholesaling. The other buyers are ultimate consumers buying or renting for personal or household use, which is retailing even when the item is the same (gloves).

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the three main categories of wholesalers in the course figure?
questions.explanation: The figure's three categories are merchant wholesalers, agents and brokers, and manufacturer's branches and offices. Retailer-sponsored cooperatives are a type of contractual retail system (e.g., Home Hardware).

questions.stem: What ultimately determines whether a sale is classified as wholesaling or retailing?
options: The buyer's purpose: resale or business use versus personal, family or household use
Whether the seller operates a physical store
Whether the price is above or below the regular price
questions.explanation: The definitions hinge on why the buyer purchases: resale or business use = wholesaling; personal, family or household use = retailing. A large order by a family is still retailing, and many retailers sell without stores.

questions.stem: Merchant wholesalers are independently owned firms that:
options: never take title and earn commissions on sales
take title to the merchandise they handle
are owned and operated by the manufacturer
only bring buyers and sellers together for single transactions
questions.explanation: Taking title (ownership) is the defining feature of merchant wholesalers. Agents and brokers do not take title and earn commissions; manufacturer's branches and offices are owned by the manufacturer.

questions.stem: Western Supply Co. carries a broad range of products (hardware, cleaning supplies, small appliances and toys) with only a few items in each line. It buys and owns the goods and offers credit, delivery and sales support to small retailers. Western Supply is a:
questions.explanation: A full-service merchant wholesaler carrying a broad range with little depth is a general merchandise wholesaler. A specialty merchandise wholesaler does the opposite: a narrow range with a deep assortment.

questions.stem: Pacific Seafood Distributors carries only seafood but offers an extremely deep assortment of fresh, frozen and specialty fish. It owns its stock and provides credit, delivery and merchandising advice to restaurants and grocers. It is a:
questions.explanation: A narrow range with a deep assortment, plus full services, marks a specialty merchandise wholesaler. A truck jobber also sells perishables, but it is a limited-service wholesaler selling for cash from a truck, not offering credit and advice.

questions.stem: A merchant wholesaler and a manufacturers' agent both sell a producer's goods to retailers. What is the key difference?
options: The agent takes title to the goods; the merchant wholesaler earns a commission
The merchant wholesaler is owned by the manufacturer; the agent is independent
The merchant wholesaler takes title to the goods; the agent does not and earns a commission
The agent always holds inventory in a branch office
questions.explanation: Title is the dividing line: merchant wholesalers buy and own the goods, while agents and brokers sell on commission without taking title. Ownership by the manufacturer describes branches and offices, not merchant wholesalers.

questions.stem: Because merchant wholesalers take title to the goods they handle, they:
options: earn only a commission on each sale
bear the risks of ownership, such as theft, damage, spoilage and obsolescence
cannot resell the goods to retailers
are considered vertical integration by the manufacturer
questions.explanation: Owning the goods means owning the risk, which is why risk bearing is a wholesaler function. Earning only commissions is what agents and brokers do, precisely because they do NOT take title.

questions.stem: What distinguishes full-service merchant wholesalers from limited-service merchant wholesalers?
options: Full-service wholesalers do not take title, while limited-service wholesalers do
Limited-service wholesalers are owned by manufacturers
Full-service wholesalers sell only to ultimate consumers
Full-service wholesalers provide a wide range of services, while limited-service wholesalers offer only a few
questions.explanation: Both groups are merchant wholesalers and both take title; they differ in how many services they perform. General and specialty merchandise wholesalers are full-service, while rack jobbers, cash and carry wholesalers, drop shippers and truck jobbers are limited-service.

questions.stem: Glossy Racks Inc. installs and stocks magazine and greeting-card displays in pharmacies. It owns the merchandise on the racks and bills each store only for the items that sell. Glossy Racks is a:
questions.explanation: Rack jobbers furnish and stock display racks in stores, own the inventory and bill only for items sold. A truck jobber sells perishables for cash from a truck rather than maintaining racks.

questions.stem: Restaurant owners visit Metro Depot's warehouse, pay for supplies on the spot and haul them away in their own vans; Metro offers no credit and no delivery. Metro Depot is a:
questions.explanation: Customers paying cash and furnishing their own transportation, with no credit or delivery, defines cash and carry wholesaling. A general merchandise wholesaler is full-service, offering credit and delivery.

questions.stem: TimberLink takes orders from builders for carloads of lumber and has the sawmill ship directly to each job site. TimberLink owns the lumber while it is in transit but never stores or handles it. TimberLink is a:
questions.explanation: Drop shippers (desk jobbers) take title but never physically handle, store or deliver the goods; the producer ships directly to the customer, typical for bulky goods like lumber. A broker also never handles goods, but a broker does not take title.

questions.stem: Fresh Daily Dairy runs a small warehouse and sends trucks along regular routes each morning, selling milk and yogurt to convenience stores for cash right off the truck. Fresh Daily is a:
questions.explanation: Truck jobbers are small wholesalers with a small warehouse that sell perishables (bakery, dairy, meat) for cash from their trucks. A rack jobber stocks and owns in-store displays and bills only for items sold.

questions.stem: Both a drop shipper and a broker can arrange a sale without ever physically handling the goods. What distinguishes them?
options: The drop shipper takes title to the goods; the broker does not
The broker takes title to the goods; the drop shipper does not
The drop shipper is owned by the manufacturer; the broker is independent
The broker always stores inventory in a warehouse
questions.explanation: A drop shipper is a merchant wholesaler, so it owns the goods even though the producer ships them directly. A broker is an agent intermediary: it brings buyers and sellers together for a commission without taking title.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a limited-service merchant wholesaler?
questions.explanation: Selling agents are agents (no title) that handle a single producer's entire marketing function. The four limited-service merchant wholesalers are rack jobbers, cash and carry wholesalers, drop shippers and truck jobbers.

questions.stem: A rack jobber is best defined as a wholesaler that:
options: owns goods but ships them directly from producer to customer without handling them
furnishes and stocks racks in stores, owns the merchandise displayed and bills only for items sold
sells perishable goods for cash directly from a truck
requires customers to pay cash and provide their own transportation
questions.explanation: That is the rack jobber definition (common for hosiery and magazines). The distractors define the drop shipper, truck jobber and cash and carry wholesaler, the other three limited-service types.

questions.stem: Ana represents four non-competing producers (a cutlery maker, a cookware maker, a linen maker and a candle maker), selling their lines to kitchen stores in an exclusive Alberta territory for a commission. Ana is a:
questions.explanation: Manufacturers' agents work for several producers, carrying non-competitive, complementary lines in an exclusive territory, and do not take title. A selling agent represents only ONE producer and handles its entire marketing function.

questions.stem: Okanagan Ridge, a small winery, contracts with Vino Sales Group to handle its entire marketing function (pricing, promotion and selling in all markets) for a commission. Vino Sales Group is a:
questions.explanation: A selling agent represents a single producer and is responsible for that producer's entire marketing function. A sales office is owned by the manufacturer itself, not an independent agent.

questions.stem: Hana connects a potato farm with a food processor for a one-time sale of surplus potatoes and earns a commission. She has no ongoing relationship with either party and never owns the potatoes. Hana is acting as a:
questions.explanation: Brokers bring buyers and sellers together to make a sale, usually with no continuous relationship (common in real estate, food and insurance). A drop shipper would take title to the potatoes, which Hana does not.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes a manufacturers' agent from a selling agent?
options: A selling agent sells non-competing lines for several producers in an exclusive territory; a manufacturers' agent handles the entire marketing function for one producer
A manufacturers' agent takes title; a selling agent does not
A manufacturers' agent sells non-competing lines for several producers in an exclusive territory; a selling agent handles the entire marketing function for one producer
A selling agent is owned by the manufacturer; a manufacturers' agent is independent
questions.explanation: The key differences are how many producers they represent and how much of the marketing they handle. Neither takes title (both are agents earning commissions), and neither is owned by the manufacturer.

questions.stem: Agents and brokers differ from merchant wholesalers because they:
options: take title to the goods and bear ownership risk
do not take title to the goods and typically earn commissions
are owned and operated by the manufacturer
questions.explanation: Agents and brokers facilitate sales without owning the goods, earning commissions instead of resale margins. Taking title and bearing risk is what merchant wholesalers do.

questions.stem: Which statement about brokers is NOT accurate?
options: Their main function is bringing buyers and sellers together
They usually have no continuous relationship with their clients
They are common in real estate, food and insurance
They take title to the goods they sell
questions.explanation: Brokers never take title; they are agent intermediaries paid commissions. The other statements match the course description of brokers.

questions.stem: Manufacturer's branches and offices are wholesaling operations that are:
options: independently owned and take title to goods
owned and operated by the manufacturer
questions.explanation: Manufacturer's branches and offices are a form of vertical integration in wholesaling: the producer owns them. Independent firms that take title are merchant wholesalers; independent commission earners are agents and brokers.

questions.stem: Polar Appliances, a manufacturer, owns a regional facility in Winnipeg that holds inventory and sells and delivers appliances to retailers across the Prairies. This facility is a:
questions.explanation: A manufacturer-owned unit that carries inventory and performs wholesaling functions is a branch office. A sales office does not carry inventory; it only performs a sales function.

questions.stem: TechCore Chips, a manufacturer, opens a small downtown Toronto office where its salespeople meet business customers and take orders. All products ship from the factory; the office holds no inventory. This is a:
questions.explanation: A manufacturer-owned sales office carries no inventory and performs only a sales function. A branch office would also store inventory and perform other wholesaling functions.

questions.stem: What is the key difference between a manufacturer's branch office and its sales office?
options: A sales office carries inventory; a branch office does not
A branch office is independently owned; a sales office is owned by the manufacturer
A sales office takes title to goods; a branch office earns commissions
A branch office carries inventory; a sales office does not and performs only a sales function
questions.explanation: Both are owned by the manufacturer; inventory is the difference. Branch = inventory plus wholesaling functions; sales office = no inventory, selling only.

questions.stem: Why might a manufacturer set up its own branch offices instead of relying on merchant wholesalers?
options: To let independent agents take title to its goods
To control wholesaling functions directly through ownership (vertical integration)
questions.explanation: Manufacturer's branches and offices represent vertical integration in wholesaling: the producer owns and controls the wholesale operation. Avoiding inventory describes a sales office, not the reason to open a branch office, which carries inventory.

questions.stem: Prairie Grocery Wholesale buys pasta by the truckload from manufacturers and resells it to small independent grocers in cases of 12. Which wholesaler function is this?
questions.explanation: Bulk breaking means buying in large quantities and dividing them into smaller lots that small customers can use. Assortment building is about bringing together a VARIETY of products, not splitting one product into smaller quantities.

questions.stem: A wholesaler lets small retailers pay for their orders 60 days after delivery. Which wholesaler function is this?
questions.explanation: Extending credit to customers is the financing function. Risk bearing is absorbing the risks of owning goods (theft, damage, spoilage, obsolescence), not giving customers time to pay.

questions.stem: A heat wave spoils a wholesaler's stock of chocolate before it can be resold, and the wholesaler absorbs the loss because it owns the goods. This reflects which wholesaler function?
questions.explanation: By taking title, wholesalers absorb risks such as spoilage, theft, damage and obsolescence; that is the risk-bearing function. Warehousing (storing goods) is where the loss happened, but absorbing the financial loss is risk bearing.

questions.stem: A wholesaler helps an independent hardware store redesign its layout, train its clerks and set up an inventory-control system. Which wholesaler function is this?
questions.explanation: Helping retailers improve operations (training, layout, accounting or inventory systems) is management services and counselling. Market information is passing along facts about competitors, new products and prices, not hands-on operational help.

questions.stem: A wholesaler tells its suppliers which competing products are gaining popularity with retailers and how prices are trending. Which wholesaler function is this?
questions.explanation: Sharing information about competitors, new products and price developments is the market information function. Management services and counselling involves helping customers run their businesses, not reporting market trends.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the nine wholesaler functions?
questions.explanation: Category management is a retailer practice (managing a product category as a strategic business unit). The nine wholesaler functions are selling and promoting, buying and assortment building, bulk breaking, warehousing, transportation, financing, risk bearing, market information, and management services and counselling.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes bulk breaking from buying and assortment building?
options: Bulk breaking divides large quantities into smaller lots; assortment building brings together a variety of products customers need
Bulk breaking brings together a variety of products; assortment building divides large quantities into smaller lots
Both refer to storing goods until customers need them
Both refer to extending credit to customers
questions.explanation: Bulk breaking is about QUANTITY (a truckload into cases); assortment building is about VARIETY (gathering many items so customers can buy from one source). Storing goods is warehousing and extending credit is financing.

questions.stem: Warehousing, transportation, financing and risk bearing are all among the nine wholesaler functions.
questions.explanation: True. The nine functions are selling and promoting; buying and assortment building; bulk breaking; warehousing; transportation; financing; risk bearing; market information; and management services and counselling.
